title: Password Power & Secret Keepers
tagline: Students rank passwords from weak to strong, build silly-but-strong practice passphrases, and sort tricky moments into keep it secret, share with a trusted grown-up, or tell a grown-up now.
groupSize: Teams of 3–4, then individuals; any number of teams
overview: By third grade, many students have school logins, game accounts, or a family tablet code. This lesson gives them three habits to protect those accounts. First, teams line up password cards from weakest to strongest and discover that long, random **passphrases** beat short passwords full of personal details. Next, they build silly practice passphrases from word cards (never their real ones). Then they become **Secret Keepers**, sorting tricky moments, including a message that asks for a password and a phone call from a voice that sounds just like a relative, into *keep it secret*, *share only with a trusted grown-up*, or *tell a grown-up now*. They leave with a plan for what to do when an account acts weird.
objectives: Students will explain what makes a password strong (long, random words, not personal information, different for each account) and rank examples.
Students will build a practice passphrase and explain why it is hard to guess but easy to remember.
Students will decide who, if anyone, can know a password in a set of scenarios, and explain why friends are not on the list.
Students will name the steps to take when an account acts weird, including telling a trusted grown-up, and one way to check a surprising call or message.

print: Handout A: Password Line-Up (1 set per team, cut apart)
Handout B: Secret Keeper Sort (1 set per team, cut apart, plus the three category labels)
Handout C: My Password Power Plan (1 per student; the last section goes home)
Word slips for building passphrases: write 30–40 fun, unrelated words (taco, rocket, purple, umbrella, giraffe, pickle, cloud, trumpet…) on scraps, and put them in a bag
Tape or a clothesline and clothespins for the password line-up (optional)
digital: Optional: the teacher's device, projected, to show where a school account's password-change and sign-out settings live (use a demo or teacher account, never a student's)
Optional: a document camera to show the line-up

prep: Print and cut Handouts A and B for each team. Keep the backs (the key) for yourself.
Write 30–40 random fun words on slips and put them in a bag or envelope. Avoid names, places, or anything personal.
Decide what your school's real rule is for who can help with a student's school password (for example, the teacher or the campus tech helper), so you can name it accurately in the Secret Keeper step.
Remind yourself of the lesson's one firm rule: students never write or say their real passwords today. Everything is practice.

steps.title: The locked diary
steps.body: Hold up a notebook and say: "This is my secret diary. It has a lock. The combination is… my birthday!" Ask: **"Is that a good lock?"** Students will say no: lots of people know your birthday. Say: "Accounts online have locks too. They're called **passwords**. Today you'll learn to make powerful ones, and to be a Secret Keeper who knows who is allowed to know them."
steps.note: Make the one firm rule clear right away: "We will never say or write our real passwords today. Everything we make is practice."

steps.title: Password Line-Up
steps.body: Teams get the ten Handout A cards and line them up (on the table or on a clothesline) from **weakest** to **strongest**. They must agree on a reason for their top and bottom card. Then reveal the key: read the backs for a few cards and have teams adjust. Build a class list of **Password Power rules** on the board: **long beats short; random words beat real words about you; no names, birthdays, pets, or teams; a different password for every account; never share it with friends.**
steps.note: Teams often rank a short password with symbols (like the "B@ddy!" card) above a long passphrase. That's the key misconception. Ask: "Which one would be harder for someone to guess if they knew a lot about you? Which one could you remember?"

steps.title: Build a practice passphrase
steps.body: Each student draws **four word slips** from the bag without looking, and writes them in the practice box on Handout C as a silly passphrase (for example, *pickle-trumpet-cloud-giraffe*). Then they draw a quick picture that helps them remember it. Say: "This is how you make a real one at home with a grown-up: random words, a funny picture in your head. But this one is only for practice. Real passwords don't go on paper at school."
steps.note: Point out why drawing without looking matters: words you choose yourself tend to be things you like, and people who know you might guess those. Random picks are harder to guess.

steps.title: Secret Keeper Sort
steps.body: Teams sort the twelve Handout B scenarios into **Keep it secret**, **Share only with a trusted grown-up**, and **Tell a grown-up now**. Circulate and ask, "Why?" Then discuss the tricky ones as a class. For the two-step check card, explain: "Some accounts send a second check, like a code to a grown-up's phone, when someone signs in. It's like a second lock. If a code shows up and you didn't try to sign in, that's a signal to tell a grown-up." For the voice card, say: "Computer tools can now copy a person's voice. A family can pick a secret **safe word** to check that a caller is really who they say they are."
steps.note: Keep the voice-copying piece calm and brief. The takeaway isn't fear; it's a family habit: hang up and check another way, or ask the safe word. Name your school's real rule for who helps with school passwords.

steps.title: When an account acts weird
steps.body: Read this aloud: "Jada logs into her game account and her avatar has new clothes she didn't buy, and her friends say she sent them strange messages." Ask teams: **"What should Jada do first? Next?"** Build the steps together: **1. Stop and don't click anything new. 2. Tell a trusted grown-up right away. 3. With the grown-up, change the password to a new, strong one. 4. Turn on a two-step check if the account has one. 5. Tell friends not to open the strange messages.** Students copy the steps they'd use into Handout C.
steps.note: Emphasize that Jada is not in trouble. Kids hide account problems when they fear punishment. Say: "Telling a grown-up fast is the smart move, every time."

steps.title: Secret Keeper pledge
steps.body: Students finish Handout C on their own: who their trusted grown-ups are for passwords, and one Password Power rule they will use this week. Collect or check it as evidence. Close by reading the family section aloud: "Tonight, talk with your family about making a safe word. Decide it together, and don't write it down on this paper."
steps.note: Students without a family phone or accounts can still do the plan: school accounts count, and a safe word works for any family.

unplugged: Everything runs on paper: the line-up cards, the word-slip bag, the sort, and the plan. The line-up works well as a movement activity: give ten students one card each and have the class arrange them across the front of the room from weakest to strongest.
digital: On the teacher's device, projected, show where a demo or teacher account keeps its password-change, sign-out-everywhere, and two-step settings, so students can recognize those words later. Never display a student's account. Students do not need devices or accounts for this lesson. For extra practice, share the Secret Keeper scenarios as a teacher-led slide poll where students vote with hand signals.
whyTech: This lesson is better unplugged: the habits are decisions and conversations, and practicing them on paper keeps real passwords off screens and out of sight. A short projected tour of real account settings earns its time by making "change your password" and "two-step check" concrete.

adaptations.label: Grade 3
adaptations.text: Use six line-up cards (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and the sort with two categories: Keep it secret and Tell a grown-up. Draw three word slips instead of four.

adaptations.label: Grade 5
adaptations.text: Add a discussion of why using the same password everywhere is risky: if one account is broken into, the others are open too. Students explain it to a partner with the diary-and-house-key comparison.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Allow word slips in home languages (a mix of languages makes a strong passphrase). Pre-teach password, secret, trusted, and code with gestures and pictures.

adaptations.label: Students with reading needs
adaptations.text: Read sort cards aloud in teams and let students sort by pointing or placing. Provide a picture icon for each category (a lock, a grown-up, a megaphone).

lookFors: Teams rank the long random passphrase above short passwords with symbols and give a reason about length or guessability.
Students sort "a best friend asks for your password" into Keep it secret and explain that friends don't need passwords, even kind ones.
Students list "tell a trusted grown-up" as an early step when an account acts weird, without suggesting they would hide it.
Students name one way to check a surprising call or message (hang up and call back on a known number, ask the safe word, ask a grown-up).
reflection: How do I protect my accounts and personal information? (Student ELE 2.1: I know how to protect my personal information online.)
Who are my trusted grown-ups for passwords, and why isn't my best friend on the list?
What will I do if something about an account, a message, or a call feels weird?
transfer: At home, students use the last section of Handout C to talk with their family about choosing a family safe word and about who helps them with passwords, and they teach a family member the passphrase trick. In a later lesson, connect to *Phish Tank IRL* to practice spotting scam messages.

handouts.title: Password Line-Up
handouts.instructions: Cut apart. Line these up from WEAKEST to STRONGEST. None of these belong to a real person. The backs are the teacher's key.

cards.label: Card 1
cards.back: Weakest. It's one of the first things anyone would guess.

cards.label: Card 2
cards.back: Very weak. Short and a famous pattern.

cards.label: Card 3
cards.front: Buddy2016 (the name of a dog and the year he was born)
cards.back: Weak. Anyone who knows the family, or sees a photo of Buddy's birthday, could guess it.

cards.label: Card 4
cards.front: B@ddy! (Buddy with a symbol swapped in)
cards.back: Still weak. Swapping a letter for a symbol is a trick people know about, and it's short.

cards.label: Card 5
cards.back: Weak. Longer, but it's easy to find out someone's school and team.

cards.label: Card 6
cards.front: Emma0412 (a first name and a birthday)
cards.back: Weak. Names and birthdays are personal information people can find.

cards.label: Card 7
cards.back: Weak. One common word, easy to guess.

cards.label: Card 8
cards.back: Strong. Four random words: long, hard to guess, and easy to remember with a silly picture.

cards.label: Card 9
cards.back: Strongest in this set. Five random words. Long beats short.

cards.label: Card 10
cards.front: The same strong passphrase used for a game, a school login, AND a video app
cards.back: Tricky! A strong password turns weak when it's reused. If one account gets broken into, the others are open too. Every account needs its own.

handouts.title: Secret Keeper Sort
handouts.instructions: Read each card. Decide: keep it secret, share only with a trusted grown-up, or tell a grown-up now. Be ready to say why.
categories: Share only with a trusted grown-up

items.text: Your best friend says, "Tell me your game password so I can help you beat the next level."
items.why: Friends, even kind ones, don't need your password. Friendships change, and it's your account.

items.text: Your mom or dad needs your password to help set up the family tablet.
items.answer: Share only with a trusted grown-up
items.why: The grown-ups who take care of you and your accounts can know it.

items.text: A pop-up in a game says, "You won 10,000 free coins! Type your password to claim them."
items.why: A real game never needs your password to give you a prize. This is a trick to steal your account.

items.text: A classmate is standing behind you watching while you type your school password.
items.why: Cover the keyboard or ask them to step back, kindly. Passwords stay private.

items.text: You get a message: "This is the Game Help Team. Your account will be deleted today unless you send your password."
items.why: Rushing you and asking for a password are scam signals. Real help teams don't ask for passwords.

items.text: Your teacher helps you reset your school login after you forgot it.
items.answer: Share only with a trusted grown-up
items.why: The grown-ups in charge of school accounts can help, following your school's rules.

items.text: A code shows up on your grandma's phone that says "Your sign-in code is 482913," but nobody in your family was trying to sign in.
items.why: That second check means someone may be trying to get into the account. Never share the code; tell a grown-up.

items.text: Someone calls. The voice sounds exactly like your uncle, and he says he's in trouble and needs your family's bank code right now.
items.why: Computer tools can copy voices. Hang up and have a grown-up call your uncle back on the number they already have, or ask for the family safe word.

items.text: A new friend in an online game asks what your password hint question is ("What's your pet's name?").
items.why: Hint answers can unlock accounts. They're secrets too.

items.text: You see your older cousin's password on a sticky note on the fridge.
items.why: Don't use it or share it. You might let your cousin know it's not a safe spot.

items.text: Your game account suddenly shows items you didn't buy and messages you didn't send.
items.why: Someone else may be using your account. Tell a grown-up fast so you can change the password together.

items.text: Your guardian wants to turn on a two-step check for your account so a code goes to their phone.
items.answer: Share only with a trusted grown-up
items.why: A second lock managed by a trusted grown-up makes your account much safer.

handouts.title: My Password Power Plan
handouts.instructions: PRACTICE ONLY. Never write a real password on this page.

sections.prompt: My practice passphrase (four random words from the bag):
Draw a silly picture that helps you remember it.
Two Password Power rules I will use:
My trusted grown-ups for passwords are:
If an account acts weird, my steps are:
If a call or message surprises me or asks for a password or code, I can check by…
Take home: talk with your family about choosing a family safe word to check that a caller is really family. Decide it together. Don't write it here! Family signature when you've talked:
